screens.title: Layer 3 Switching and Inter‑VLAN Routing
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will see how a multi-layer switch combines high-speed switching with routing to solve the performance limits of the classic router-on-a-stick layout. You will learn what a Switched Virtual Interface is, how to enable global ip routing, when to use a routed port, and how to advertise VLAN networks with OSPF. For example, we’ll configure SVIs for VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 with addresses 192.168.10.1 and 192.168.20.1, enable ip routing, and then create a routed port to an uplink running OSPF. Understanding this matters because routing at the switch backplane removes the single-trunk bottleneck of router-on-a-stick and gives wire‑speed inter‑VLAN forwarding. A common misconception is that SVIs alone provide routing — they do not unless ip routing is enabled. As you explore the topic visually, keep an eye out for the verification steps: show ip route, show ip interface brief, and show ip ospf neighbor. By the end you will be able to configure basic inter‑VLAN routing on a multi-layer switch and verify connectivity to external networks.

screens.title: Router‑on‑a‑Stick vs Layer 3 Switching
screens.narratorSegment: Start by understanding the classic router‑on‑a‑stick layout. In that design a router connects to a Layer 2 switch via a single trunk. The router uses subinterfaces — one per VLAN — to route between VLANs. While simple, this funnels all inter‑VLAN traffic across one trunk link and through the router C P U, which can create a throughput bottleneck in busy networks. Contrast that with a multi‑layer switch, which performs routing on the switch backplane using hardware forwarding. The switch has SVIs, one per VLAN, that act as Layer 3 gateways and exchange traffic locally at wire speed. Choose router‑on‑a‑stick for very small or lab setups where performance is not required. Choose Layer 3 switching for enterprise access and distribution where many VLANs and high throughput matter. A common mistake is assuming both provide identical performance; they do not. Also, remember that design choices affect troubleshooting: with router‑on‑a‑stick, the trunk and router subinterfaces are first suspects; with Layer 3 switching, check SVIs, ip routing, and access port VLAN assignment. Reflect: which approach aligns with your network scale and performance needs?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Router-on-a-stick vs MLS
Router-on-a-stick
Single trunk to router. Subinterfaces carry VLANs; all inter‑VLAN traffic transits that trunk and router CPU.
When to use
Small labs or simple topologies where performance isn't critical.
Common pitfall
Expecting wire‑speed routing. The trunk can become a bottleneck.
Example
Router subinterfaces like Gig0/0.10 and Gig0/0.20 route between VLANs over one physical link.
Multi‑Layer Switch (Layer 3 switching)
SVIs provide local gateways and routing occurs on the switch backplane, enabling high throughput between VLANs.
When to use
Enterprise access/distribution with many VLANs and high inter‑VLAN traffic.
Strength
Wire‑speed routing on the switch backplane; less latency and higher throughput.
Example
SVI configuration: interface Vlan10 ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0; interface Vlan20 ip address 192.168.20.1 255.255.255.0.

screens.title: Switched Virtual Interface (SVI)
screens.narratorSegment: An SVI is a logical Layer 3 interface on a multi‑layer switch that represents a VLAN in IP routing. Think of it as the virtual router interface for that VLAN: hosts in VLAN 10 use the SVI IP as their default gateway. To create one you enter interface VlanX and assign an IP address, then make sure the SVI is up with no shutdown. However, an SVI alone does not enable routing — the switch must have ip routing enabled globally for SVIs to forward between VLANs. For example, configure interface Vlan10 with 192.168.10.1/24 and interface Vlan20 with 192.168.20.1/24, enable ip routing, and hosts on each subnet will be able to reach each other through the switch. A frequent mistake is failing to associate access ports with the correct VLAN, meaning hosts cannot reach their SVI. Remember to verify SVI state with show ip interface brief and the interface-specific state with show interface Vlan10. Key takeaway: SVIs are logical gateways; ip routing makes them active routers. Switched Virtual Interface (SVI) means an svi is the logical ip gateway for a vlan; ip routing must be enabled for inter‑vlan forwarding.. In practical terms, what an svi is and how it functions as a vlan gateway. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

SVI — logical VLAN gateway
Creates a Layer 3 interface tied to a VLAN so hosts have a default gateway.
Create an SVI

screens.title: Configuring SVIs and Access Ports
screens.narratorSegment: Follow a clear sequence when configuring inter‑VLAN routing. Step one: enable ip routing at the global configuration level. This single command turns the switch into a Layer 3 device capable of forwarding between SVIs. Step two: create VLANs and SVIs for each required subnet. For our lab create VLAN 10 and VLAN 20, then configure interface Vlan10 with IP 192.168.10.1/24 and interface Vlan20 with IP 192.168.20.1/24. Step three: assign physical access ports to their VLANs, for example set Gi1/0/1 as an access port in VLAN 10 and Gi1/0/2 in VLAN 20. Ensuring hosts are in the right VLAN is often the missing step when connectivity fails. Step four: confirm SVI and port states using show ip interface brief and ping from a host to its gateway. If pings fail while SVIs show up/up, recheck the switchport access vlan setting. This process prevents common misconfigurations and produces a reproducible lab workflow you can use during testing and verification. Configuring SVIs and Access Ports means enable ip routing, create svis, assign access ports to vlans, then verify with show ip interface brief and basic pings.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Configuring SVIs
Step-by-step
Follow these steps in the lab to create SVIs and assign access ports.
1. Enable routing
ip routing
2. Create VLANs
vlan 10 name Users_VLAN; vlan 20 name Servers_VLAN
3. Configure SVIs
interface Vlan10
 ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
 no shutdown
!
interface Vlan20
 ip address 192.168.20.1 255.255.255.0
 no shutdown
4. Assign access ports
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/1 switchport mode access switchport access vlan 10
Verification & tips
Use show ip interface brief to confirm SVIs are up/up. Ping the SVI from a host to confirm layer 3 reachability. If SVI is up but pings fail, check the access port VLAN assignment; hosts must be in the same VLAN as the SVI.
Pro tip
Always configure no shutdown on SVIs and remember that SVIs do not appear in the routing table unless ip routing is enabled globally.

screens.title: Routed Ports and When to Use Them
screens.narratorSegment: Routed ports are physical switch interfaces that operate as Layer 3 interfaces after you configure no switchport. Once converted, you can assign an IP address directly to the port and enable routing protocols on it like any router interface. Routed ports are useful for point‑to‑point connections to a core router, firewall, or another switch where Layer 2 switching on that link is unnecessary. For example, configure Gi1/0/3 with no switchport and ip address 10.0.0.1 255.255.255.252 to create a /30 link to an upstream router. Routed ports simplify topologies where you do not want bridging on a link and can reduce the number of SVIs needed. A misconception is that routed ports replace the need for SVIs; they do not — they serve different purposes. Use routed ports for uplinks and SVIs for VLAN gateways. Always verify routed port status with show ip interface brief and include the routed subnet in your routing protocol advertisements so the rest of the network learns the path. Routed Ports and When to Use Them means use no switchport to create a layer 3 point‑to‑point link; advertise its network so peers can route to it.. screens.title: OSPF on a Multi‑Layer Switch
screens.narratorSegment: When a multi‑layer switch must communicate with external networks, you can run a routing protocol such as OSPF on the switch just as you would on a router. After enabling ip routing and configuring SVIs and routed ports, enter router ospf 1 and add network statements that match your subnets. For the lab we advertise 192.168.10.0/24, 192.168.20.0/24 and the routed 10.0.0.0/30 network into area 0. The switch will then form OSPF adjacencies over the routed port or any other routed interfaces and exchange LSAs, allowing other routers to learn the SVI networks. A common troubleshooting step is checking show ip ospf neighbor to confirm adjacencies and show ip route to confirm learned routes. Misconfigurations often come from missing network statements or using incorrect wildcard masks. Remember that SVIs are locally connected networks and will appear as connected in the routing table; OSPF ensures those networks are known to the wider routing domain. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will see how a multi-layer switch combines high-speed switching with routing to solve the performance limits of the classic router-on-a-stick layout. You will learn what a Switched Virtual Interface is, how to enable global ip routing, when to use a routed port, and how to advertise VLAN networks with OSPF. For example, we’ll configure SVIs for VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 with addresses 192.168.10.1 and 192.168.20.1, enable ip routing, and then create a routed port to an uplink running OSPF. Understanding this matters because routing at the switch backplane removes the single-trunk bottleneck of router-on-a-stick and gives wire‑speed inter‑VLAN forwarding. A common misconception is that SVIs alone provide routing — they do not unless ip routing is enabled. As you explore the topic visually, keep an eye out for the verification steps: show ip route, show ip interface brief, and show ip ospf neighbor. By the end you will be able to configure basic inter‑VLAN routing on a multi-layer switch and verify connectivity to external networks.

Over the next screens you will gain four practical skills that let you build and troubleshoot inter‑VLAN routing on a multi‑layer switch. First, you will explain Layer 3 switching and why it outperforms a router-on-a-stick. Understanding the hardware and forwarding behavior clarifies design decisions. Second, you will create and configure SVIs so each VLAN has a logical default gateway, and you will learn the exact commands used in a hands-on lab. Third, you will enable and verify routing protocols on a switch, such as OSPF, to exchange routes with an external router; this includes advertising SVI networks and a routed port. Fourth, you will use troubleshooting checks like show ip route and show ip interface brief to diagnose SVI and routing problems. Each objective includes a short mnemonic or visual to help you remember the steps and a verified competency milestone so you can measure readiness. By focusing on these four outcomes you move from conceptual understanding to operational skill.

This checklist prepares you for the hands-on lab steps. First, you will enable ip routing on a multi-layer switch. That single global command allows SVIs to exchange routes. Second, you will create VLANs and configure interface Vlan10 and Vlan20 with their IP addresses so hosts have correct default gateways. Third, you will convert a physical interface to a routed port using no switchport and assign it an IP address to connect to an external router. Fourth, you will configure OSPF process 1 and advertise the SVI and routed port networks so the switch can learn and share routes. Each checklist item has a brief explanation and a verification command to run after configuration. Practicing these tasks ensures you can both build a working topology and diagnose why inter-VLAN traffic might fail.

Start by understanding the classic router‑on‑a‑stick layout. In that design a router connects to a Layer 2 switch via a single trunk. The router uses subinterfaces — one per VLAN — to route between VLANs. While simple, this funnels all inter‑VLAN traffic across one trunk link and through the router C P U, which can create a throughput bottleneck in busy networks. Contrast that with a multi‑layer switch, which performs routing on the switch backplane using hardware forwarding. The switch has SVIs, one per VLAN, that act as Layer 3 gateways and exchange traffic locally at wire speed. Choose router‑on‑a‑stick for very small or lab setups where performance is not required. Choose Layer 3 switching for enterprise access and distribution where many VLANs and high throughput matter. A common mistake is assuming both provide identical performance; they do not. Also, remember that design choices affect troubleshooting: with router‑on‑a‑stick, the trunk and router subinterfaces are first suspects; with Layer 3 switching, check SVIs, ip routing, and access port VLAN assignment. Reflect: which approach aligns with your network scale and performance needs?

An SVI is a logical Layer 3 interface on a multi‑layer switch that represents a VLAN in IP routing. Think of it as the virtual router interface for that VLAN: hosts in VLAN 10 use the SVI IP as their default gateway. To create one you enter interface VlanX and assign an IP address, then make sure the SVI is up with no shutdown. However, an SVI alone does not enable routing — the switch must have ip routing enabled globally for SVIs to forward between VLANs. For example, configure interface Vlan10 with 192.168.10.1/24 and interface Vlan20 with 192.168.20.1/24, enable ip routing, and hosts on each subnet will be able to reach each other through the switch. A frequent mistake is failing to associate access ports with the correct VLAN, meaning hosts cannot reach their SVI. Remember to verify SVI state with show ip interface brief and the interface-specific state with show interface Vlan10. Key takeaway: SVIs are logical gateways; ip routing makes them active routers. Switched Virtual Interface (SVI) means an svi is the logical ip gateway for a vlan; ip routing must be enabled for inter‑vlan forwarding.. In practical terms, what an svi is and how it functions as a vlan gateway. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Follow a clear sequence when configuring inter‑VLAN routing. Step one: enable ip routing at the global configuration level. This single command turns the switch into a Layer 3 device capable of forwarding between SVIs. Step two: create VLANs and SVIs for each required subnet. For our lab create VLAN 10 and VLAN 20, then configure interface Vlan10 with IP 192.168.10.1/24 and interface Vlan20 with IP 192.168.20.1/24. Step three: assign physical access ports to their VLANs, for example set Gi1/0/1 as an access port in VLAN 10 and Gi1/0/2 in VLAN 20. Ensuring hosts are in the right VLAN is often the missing step when connectivity fails. Step four: confirm SVI and port states using show ip interface brief and ping from a host to its gateway. If pings fail while SVIs show up/up, recheck the switchport access vlan setting. This process prevents common misconfigurations and produces a reproducible lab workflow you can use during testing and verification. Configuring SVIs and Access Ports means enable ip routing, create svis, assign access ports to vlans, then verify with show ip interface brief and basic pings.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Routed ports are physical switch interfaces that operate as Layer 3 interfaces after you configure no switchport. Once converted, you can assign an IP address directly to the port and enable routing protocols on it like any router interface. Routed ports are useful for point‑to‑point connections to a core router, firewall, or another switch where Layer 2 switching on that link is unnecessary. For example, configure Gi1/0/3 with no switchport and ip address 10.0.0.1 255.255.255.252 to create a /30 link to an upstream router. Routed ports simplify topologies where you do not want bridging on a link and can reduce the number of SVIs needed. A misconception is that routed ports replace the need for SVIs; they do not — they serve different purposes. Use routed ports for uplinks and SVIs for VLAN gateways. Always verify routed port status with show ip interface brief and include the routed subnet in your routing protocol advertisements so the rest of the network learns the path. Routed Ports and When to Use Them means use no switchport to create a layer 3 point‑to‑point link; advertise its network so peers can route to it.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Here is a practical configuration template you can paste into a lab device. Start with ip routing to enable Layer 3 functions. Let’s review common misconfigurations and how they show up. First, forgetting to enable ip routing: symptoms include SVIs appearing in show ip interface brief but no inter‑VLAN traffic passes and show ip route only shows directly connected networks without inter‑VLAN routing. Second, access ports in the wrong VLAN: hosts cannot reach their default gateway and their pings to the SVI fail; check switchport access vlan on the physical interface. Third, SVIs administratively shut down: the SVI will be down/down — remedy with no shutdown. Fourth, incorrect OSPF network statements or wildcard masks: OSPF adjacency does not form, visible via show ip ospf neighbor; verify the network statements and IP addressing on the routed port. Lastly, mistaking routed ports for SVIs: routed ports are physical interfaces with IPs and not tied to VLANs. Let’s summarize the essential concepts to retain. Layer 3 switching lets a multi‑layer switch combine high‑speed Layer 2 switching with Layer 3 routing capabilities, often implemented in hardware for wire‑speed forwarding. An SVI is the logical interface for a VLAN and serves as the default gateway for hosts in that VLAN, but SVIs only route if ip routing is enabled globally. A routed port is a physical interface converted with no switchport and used for point‑to‑point Layer 3 links. Finally, when integrating with external networks use a routing protocol such as OSPF to advertise SVI and routed port networks so the wider domain learns them. Keep in mind the verification commands and the common troubleshooting order so you can diagnose problems quickly. These core ideas give you a practical framework to build scalable, high‑performance enterprise layer 3 designs.

Keep three quick reminders in front of you as you configure and troubleshoot. First, always enable ip routing before expecting SVIs to forward — SVIs without ip routing will not route. Second, verify access ports are in the correct VLAN; mismatched port VLANs are a frequent cause of host-to-gateway failures. Third, when connecting to the wider network use a routed port and OSPF network statements so the switch advertises its VLANs; verify with show ip ospf neighbor and show ip route. These three checks are the fastest way to rule out the majority of inter‑VLAN problems and will speed up your lab and production troubleshooting alike.
